CI phases

scripts/ci.mjs

In call order, read out of main(). A fast phase also runs on --fast and in the pre-push hook; the rest only on a full run.

01
hygienefast

Everything here is about the difference between THIS working copy and a fresh clone.

02
structurefast

The architecture rules, run over this repo's own apps and packages with the same engine `fli check` gives a client app.

03
registersfast

The three registers, graded against the rules they state about themselves.

04
snapshotsfast

A snapshot is a generated artefact committed beside its source, so a change nothing else in the repo can see arrives as a diff: the access rules enforced below the API, the DDL every hand-written statement binds to, the JSON Schema three packages validate…

05
accessfast

What did this branch do to who may do what.

06
coveragefast

Skipped is not passed. The aggregate `--filter '*'` walks straight past a package with no `test` script and prints nothing at all about it.

07
registryfast

Scaffolds an app, packs the working tree into it, installs and builds it.

08
advisoriesfast

Dependency posture, decided the way everything else here is decided: a phase, not a bot (`IDEAS/tooling-decisions.md` 5).

09
scaffoldfast
10
typecheckfast

Two halves: the direction of the ratchet (a git question) and the count itself (each package's own script already answers that, and exits 1 above its ceiling).

11
deployfull run

`fli new` → `fli make:deploy` → `fli deploy:local`: does the deploy pipeline containerise a real app? ~30s and it needs a Docker daemon, so it sits in the full tier rather than the pre-push one.

12
testsfull run

Sequential on purpose: several suites bind ports and start real servers, and interleaved output from four different runners is unreadable when one fails.

FJS-479 toolbelt singularize stripped es from every -ses plural, so a service named for a -se noun had no @@gate and no validation 2026-08-24 singularize('purchases') answered purchas. The -ses branch stripped es for every word, which is right for statuses → status and wrong for the rest of the language: cases → cas, releases → releas, licenses → licens, expenses → expens, responses → respons, databases → databas, warehouses → warehous, leases → leas, houses → hous, phases → phas, courses → cours. A round-trip test cannot see it — pluralize('cas') is cases, so both directions agree on a word that is not one, and the spec asserted the round trip. /inflect is Invariant 2's one owner and junction's deriveModelName is a caller: accessorCandidates('purchases') answered ['purchases', 'purchas'], neither matched purchase, and gateLevels reads a lookup miss as no @@gate declared. Measured against a real Litestone client, not a stand-in: a find on a service named purchases over model Purchase { @@gate("4") } passed gateAuthAround with no caller at all, where the identical posts/Post pair answered 401. resolveDefsKey fails open the same way, so autoValidate also does nothing. Not a hypothetical spelling: Purchase, Release, License, Expense, Response, Database, Warehouse, Case, Lease, Course, Phase are ordinary model names. Nothing in this repo caught it because no app here has a model ending in -se — the whole class was unreachable from the tree's own schemas. Found by putting a real ERP's 188-model schema through litestone (packages/litestone/test/fixtures/scale/openmrp.lite), where a taskleases table became model TaskLeas. Fixed 2026-08-24: strip one s by default, strip es for an -ss stem, and name the closed list of singulars that genuinely end in a bare s (status, bus, lens, …) — a list rather than a rule because status and cas both end in a vowel plus s and no ending can separate them. 22 pairs asserted both directions. FJS-482 mesa · cli A component could declare the compiler's own calling convention — function anchor(){} threw at mount and const prev = 9 rendered [object Object] 2026-08-24 anchor and props are the component function's parameters, block is threaded into every track() call, and prev is the render callback's. None was in BUILTINLOCALS, so an author could declare any of them at the top level of a script — where the declaration lands in the SAME scope and wins. Unlike FJS-471's builtins this is a shadow rather than a redeclaration, so the output is valid JavaScript and the failure moves to runtime or nowhere: function anchor(){} compiles, parses, and throws at mount with anchor.before is not a function; const prev = 9 compiles and renders [object Object], silently, because the callback's parameter shadows the author's constant. function block(), function props() and class dev {} survived the cases probed — dev is $$runtime.dev, a property rather than a scope name, and cannot be shadowed at all. Fixed by reserving the four, which refuses the declaration rather than renaming anything: the names are protocol (jetty's build plugin matches anchor, props, block as text — FJS-481), so moving them is FJS-D134's decision and not this one. The message is split by kind, because the existing one says the compiler injects it into the same scope, and two declarations is a SyntaxError and that is the wrong sentence here — nothing is injected and there is no SyntaxError. A nested scope is deliberately untouched: a parameter of the author's own function shadows nothing of the compiler's. 5 cases in emission.test.js. The open remainder is the naming decision itself — FJS-470 closed saying anchor/block/props did not converge on $$ and that half stays open below, and there was no row below: it was tracked nowhere until this one. The population is three kinds, which is what the convergence framing missed — the calling convention (four names, author-reachable, this issue), runtime PROPERTIES ($$runtime.dev, n.resolving, unshadowable), and generated locals inside emitted callbacks. Only the first group can collide, three of its four are protocol, and with them reserved the four-line rule is broken in appearance rather than in consequence
FJS-478 mesa bind:class on an element compiled to a write on a DOM property that does not exist, so neither direction ever touched the element 2026-08-24 VISION § 10.8 documented class passthrough as two shorthand forms — {class} one-way and bind:class two-way, for components that mutate their own class set and want the parent to observe the change. The second one has never worked. bind:class and its :class alias parse into bind:class={$class} and then take the form-value path, whose generic branch is const handler = () => set(el[name]) plus createEffect(() => { el[name] = readFn() ?? '' }). With name === 'class' that is el['class'], and there is no such DOM property — it is className. Measured against a real DOM: after el.class = 'raised', getAttribute('class') and className both still read own hash and only el.class reads back raised, which is a JS expando nothing renders. So the write reached nothing and the read-back read its own write. Clean compile, valid JavaScript, a binding that silently does not exist. Nothing caught it because nothing used it — zero .mesa files in this repo, across packages/ui's 69 components and every app — and compiler.test.js had a case that PINNED it: bind:class in child auto-wires $class, asserting bindInput was emitted, which is precisely the broken output. The test passed for as long as the feature was broken. Refused rather than fixed, 2026-08-24. The refusal names {class} and says why. Fixing it would be a different feature: the observe direction needs a MutationObserver on attributes, which is a mechanism nobody wrote, for a use case with no user. No comparable framework offers a two-way class binding — Svelte has class:name and the clsx-style class, Vue merges class through fallthrough attributes automatically and reserves v-model for form input, Angular has [class.x] and [(ngModel)] — and where a framework DOES observe element state it makes the binding readonly, which is what Svelte's bind:clientWidth is. If the observe direction is ever wanted it is a readonly binding with a new name, not a repair of this one. On a COMPONENT bind:class is untouched and is an ordinary two-way prop through bindProp; the refusal is on the element path alone, which is the only route to bindInput(el, 'class', …). RULE 31b in VISION, 4 cases in emission.test.js covering the accepted surface and the three refused spellings, and the pinning test replaced with the refusal. Green: mesa 1285 + 82 + 47, sierra 1089, ui 857
FJS-477 mesa A compiled door member emitted a reference to a local nothing declared — $.mounted worked in one spelling out of four and $.context.use in none 2026-08-24 $.mounted, $.context and $.inspect are the three door members that are COMPILED rather than read: a pre-parse AST pass rewrites $.x to $x, and the local that identifier resolves to is emitted only where a sniff found the shape the compiler knows how to wire. The sniff for $mounted was a regex over the script text demanding const NAME = $mounted(, so three other spellings rewrote to $mounted and emitted a reference to a binding that was never declared — $.mounted(fn) as a bare call, const m = $.mounted, and {$.mounted} in a template. Clean compile, valid JavaScript, ReferenceError on first render, which is Invariant 15's failure in its exact shape. $.context had the same hole in a wider form: the compiler consumes the SUGAR (const v = $.context.k becomes a $$ctxRead + trackDerived, $.context.k = v becomes a $$ctxProvide) and passes the runtime object through untouched — so $.context.use('k') and $.context.provide('k', fn), which are a real export (runtime.js's context = { use, provide }), emitted $context.use(…) against an undeclared $context. Every documented imperative use of context was broken and nothing in the repo used it. A template made it worse rather than the same: the rewrite is script-only, so {$.context.k} reached output verbatim and read .k off { use, provide } — undefined where the door member existed, a TypeError where it did not. Not a regression from FJS-D132 — $mounted(fn) as a bare call failed identically before the door — but the bare spelling is refused now, so $. is the only way in and it invites three spellings that do not work. Fixed 2026-08-24. The gate reads the AST the rewrite produced instead of the text: refuseCompiledDoorMisuse blesses the shapes the compiler wires and refuses every surviving $mounted by name with the working spelling stated, and answers whether a $context reference survived the sugar — which is what now requires the local, so both imperative forms work anywhere. refuseCompiledDoorInTemplate refuses $.mounted and the $.context.<key> sugar in a template, naming the script form; .use/.provide pass. The first cut of the template rule was a text scan and it refused a REPL example whose markup contains the sentence It provides $.context.count — prose about the framework is what an example page is made of. Both template scans now read templateExpressions(), every { … } region by brace depth, which also closed the same latent trap in refuseBareBuiltins. Also removed: findContextInBody, a dead validator in pass 5 carrying a live ReferenceError on an out-of-scope n — unreachable, so it had never fired. 12 cases in emission.test.js, negative-controlled (7 red with the fix neutered). FJS-458 junction Service autoload defaults to services/ beside the ENTRY, which is not where the layout the framework documents and scaffolds puts them — and the miss is silent 2026-08-23 autoload-services resolves dirname(Bun.main)/services when neither opts.autoload nor junction.services.dir is set. That is the FLAT layout, where the entry and the services are siblings. The canonical layout (root README § Project Structure, and what fli new writes) puts the entry at api/index.ts and the services at api/src/services/, so the default resolves to api/services — a directory that is not there. Nothing fails: autoloadServices is not called, the app boots, /health answers, and every route those services would have mounted is a 404. Measured on example while moving it to the canonical layout: the boot line went from services=12 to services=3 (the three auth registers, which are not autoloaded), the app came up clean, and the drive's only symptom was api never answered on /api/products — a URL that is a 404 rather than a refusal. fli new does not hit this because makeJunctionConfig declares services.dir explicitly, which means the default is unreachable for a scaffolded app and load-bearing for every hand-written or regenerated one. Three candidate fixes: fall back to dirname(Bun.main)/src/services when the sibling directory is absent; resolve against the app root rather than the entry; or keep the default and WARN by name when the resolved directory does not exist, which is the cheap half and the one that makes the other two safe to argue about. A directory that is simply absent is currently indistinguishable from an app that declares no services on purpose, and the app's own surface.snapshot.md cannot see it either — junction surface is passed --services by hand

Measured live in example: a litestone studio --schema schema.lite --port 8502 started from example/db/ had been serving example/db/db/shop.db — 4,096 bytes, one empty header page — for 19 hours, while the real database sat two directories up at 196,608 bytes. Studio showed empty tables and nothing anywhere said why. Two more of the same shape were beside it: example/web/db/shop.db, from a command run in the web root, which is where sierra's own commands are documented to run; and example/development.db, from litestone's no-config default (cli.js ./development.db). All three were invisible, which is what makes this S2 rather than an annoyance — the root .gitignore's .db matches at any depth, so git status is clean and the only way to find them is to go looking. The schema carries a comment warning about exactly this for its audit block and nothing acts on it. Three candidate fixes and they are not the same change: resolve against the schema file's directory, which is a behaviour change and is probably right (a path written beside the seed means beside the seed); refuse to open a database whose resolved path is outside the app root; or warn, which is the cheap half — fli's core/db-preflight.js already parses that path for its own reasons, though it cannot cover litestone's own CLI, which is what produced all three of these. Junk cleaned 2026-08-23; the studio's copy survives while its process holds it open. Measured again 2026-08-23 in a new tool and with a worse consequence: vite build on example/site runs from the SURFACE root, so ./db/shop.db resolved to example/site/db/shop.db — a fresh empty database, minted by the build — and the storefront prerendered 12 product pages as 0 products, exit 0. A published static site with no products in it, and nothing anywhere said why; the only reason it was caught is that the drive counts emitted pages against a query. A prerendered artefact is the sharpest version of this, because it is public the moment it ships and cannot be recalled. Worked around in the app (SHOPDBPATH=../db/shop.db on build:site and dev:site), which is a per-app patch and not the fix

The DDL is emitted, the run reaches SQLite, and the boot dies on index idxnotedeletedAt already exists — an error naming a physical index, about a schema that passed validation with no warning. Eight lines reproduce it: model Note { id Int @id body String deletedAt DateTime? @@index([deletedAt]) @@softDelete }. Declaring an index on the soft-delete column is the obvious thing to do for anyone who has not read that the attribute already does it, and it is what an introspected schema produces — found converting a real MySQL schema, where the source table had exactly that index. Two ways out and they differ: refuse at parse, naming the attribute that already provides it, or dedupe at emit and say nothing. Refused at parse, 2026-08-24. The declaration buys nothing either way — a declared index on a soft-delete table is already given the WHERE "deletedAt" IS NULL clause, so it compiled to exactly the index @@softDelete was about to write, and what a dedupe would preserve is the ability to write a line with no effect. FJS-471 mesa Nine compiler-injected builtin names emit invalid JavaScript when an author declares them with const, var or function, and the compile reports no error The builtins are injected into the component init function as a run of const declarations — const $option = { props: props }, const $slots = $runtime.makeSlots(block), const $onMount = $runtime.$onMount and their neighbours. An author who declares the same name at script top level gets a second declaration in the same scope, which is a duplicate-binding SyntaxError. Measured across four declaration forms × thirteen names, compiling and then parsing the output with acorn as sourceType: 'module': let is safe on every name, because a reactive let is renamed to $$sig<name> before emit; const, var and function each produce invalid output on nine — $option, $slots, $onMount, $onDestroy, $onCleanup, $props, $attributes, $context, $emit — for 27 silently-invalid combinations. Negative control: $zzz and a plain identifier compile and parse in all four forms, and the compiler INTERNALS ($runtime, $dom, $class, $parentElement) are clean in all four, so the surface is exactly the injected builtin set and not the $-prefixed internals. The compile reports errors: none in all 27, which is Invariant 15 exactly — a clean compile is not proof of valid JS — so the failure surfaces as a parse error in generated code in the browser, pointing at a line the author did not write. const $context = … is the plausible trigger: an author aliasing the context object locally is a natural thing to reach for, and it is one of the nine. FJS-D132 retires this class by construction rather than by patching it — one injected name instead of twelve, and a shadow of $ is one of the three refusals that ruling already requires — but the fix is worth landing FIRST and on its own, because it is small, it is the only part of that work with a user-visible defect behind it, it builds the refusal machinery the ruling needs later, and it is valuable whether or not the namespace change proceeds. The test must PARSE the emitted output, not merely assert a clean compile; asserting the compile is what let this run. Filed S3 rather than S2 because the trigger requires the author to pick one of nine specific names; the cost once triggered is S2-shaped — silent at compile, loud and misdirected at runtime Fixed 2026-08-23. BUILTINLOCALS names the thirteen injected names beside RESERVEDWORDS, and analyzeScript walks its own ast.body — not vars, which carries neither function nor class declarations, both of which collided — refusing every declaration form by name. It THROWS rather than pushing to errors, because the call site downgrades that whole array to warnings and a module that does not parse is not a warning. Scoped to the factory, so a nested const $props is still legal; over-refusing there would break code that never collided. Verified 65/65 refusals across five declaration forms including destructuring, with eight controls still compiling and parsing. Seven cases added to test/emission.test.js. Green: mesa 1233 vitest + 82 runtime-browser + 47 vite-browser, @frontierjs/ui 857 with 69/69 components opened. The surface was found to be 13 names rather than the 9 first measured — $inspect collides only when debug !== false, and $ctxProvide/$ctxRead only where $context is in use, which is why the reserved set is keyed off what the compiler MAY inject rather than what a given config does inject
FJS-483 cli · litestone · auth · basecamp Nothing detected an app that pastes a package's models instead of importing them, and a paste drifts in silence 2026-08-24 extend model (2026-08-24) removed the REASON to paste: an app can import @frontierjs/auth/schema.lite and still add the relation back to its own User, @@log(audit) and @@tenant(none). What it did not do is stop the paste, and the cost of one is measured rather than argued — basecamp carried hand copies of four auth models for its whole life, and one of them had @guarded(all) where the package writes @secret, so turning OAuth on there would have stored every provider access and refresh token unencrypted. 137 tests were green either side of the divergence, because nothing anywhere compares a copy to its original. Filed with the wrong rule in mind, and that was the whole difficulty. An app declares model X where a dependency also declares model X fires on every correct install: @frontierjs/auth ships one file to be IMPORTED and one — User — to be APPENDED and grown, so the copy itself decides nothing, and the filed note concluded a package needed a new way to say which was which. It does not. What is decidable is a column THE PACKAGE DECLARES, declared differently here. Adding a column is what an app is for; adding @@tenant(none) or a policy is the app's business too; changing the package's own column is the class that costs something. No manifest key, no language change, no parser — a line scan over a file in nodemodules, reached through that package's own exports map. Fixed 2026-08-24 as fli check's twenty-seventh rule, package-model-drift. A WARNING and not an error, because a deviation can be right and the reader has to judge: both declarations are printed, and check-baseline.json is how an app accepts one it has argued for. Its first run on basecamp found three things and closed all three, one of them in the package rather than the app. (1) User.emailVerified and (2) User.role had lost @allow('write', auth().isAdmin) — basecamp gates update at USER(4) with @@allow('update', id == auth().id), your own row, so the field policy is the only thing between a caller and their own emailVerified, and marking your own address verified is skipping the verification. Latent rather than live: basecamp exposes no users service and its gate grades on status and WorkspaceMember.role, neither of which is this — it becomes real the day a profile screen writes through a service over db.user. Both restored, and both now appear in db/access.snapshot.md, so a future removal is a diff. (3) User.accountId was String? against auth's Int? — and here the PACKAGE was wrong: every id @frontierjs/auth declares is a uuid, so an Int? could not hold one, which is what made the column unusable for the one app that reached for it. auth ships String? now; SessionContext.accountId was always a string either way. Seven cases in tests/checks.test.js, mutation-checked both directions — never comparing, and comparing the APP's columns instead of the package's (the false-positive shape), each turn it red. Green: cli 848, auth 244, basecamp 143 + 301/301
FJS-456 sierra A prerendered site's sitemap.xml lists no dynamic page, so a storefront's sitemap omits every product 2026-08-23 generateSitemap is handed routeTable.indexed, which is filtered to exclude dynamic routes — correct for an SPA, where /products/:slug/ is not a URL — and the static build then emits one file per getStaticPaths() entry and tells the sitemap nothing about them. Measured on example/site: 15 pages emitted, sitemap.xml (3 URLs) — /, /404/, /catalog/ — so the twelve pages the site exists to publish are the twelve it does not list. (/404/ being IN it is a second, smaller wrong: a not-found page is the one page that should never be indexed.) The build already has the answer — prerenderRoutes returns written, one relative path per emitted page — so the shape of the fix is to merge those in. What stops it being a two-line change is the FILTER: indexed also drops status: draft and robots: noindex, and those are declared on the ROUTE, so a dynamic route marked noindex must not have its twelve pages appear just because they were emitted. That needs the emitted paths to carry their route id, which written does not. Related and not the same: a static build also emits the SPA entry bundle, which no prerendered page links — dist/index.html is overwritten by the prerendered home page — so a static target ships a client bundle nothing loads. Whether that should be emitted at all is the same question asked about a different artefact

FJS-470 mesa Mesa carries three internal naming conventions with no principle between them, so $foo cannot be promised as an ordinary user name 2026-08-24 FJS-D132 folds the twelve author-facing builtins onto one $ object and deliberately leaves the compiler internals where they are, which means the rule it establishes is only two-thirds true. Three prefixes are in use and the split is historical rather than designed: single $ holds the per-instance frame locals ($runtime 217 emit sites, $dom 82, $option 37, $parentElement 31, $class 29, $domFirst 18, $domLast 7 — 421 in all), $$ holds roughly 150 uses across $$sig, $$proxy, $$watch, $$set, $$snippet, $$item, $$v, $$e, $$arg0 plus the $$eachBlock / $$virtualEach / $$delegate runtime exports, and holds 132 more in block, anchor, dev, props. A shape is discernible in the $$ tier — it wears two dollars precisely where a name is generated from a user identifier or injected into a scope the author's own code runs in, which is the collision-avoidance job — but nothing enforces it and the single-$ frame locals are in author scope too. The fix is to converge on $$, not on . runtime would say the internals are generic JavaScript noise; $$runtime says same family, one layer down, and it leaves the four-line rule true end to end: $ is the door, $: / $name: is the label, $$ is the compiler's, everything else is yours. It also converts FJS-D132's deferred win into a delivered one — $foo becomes an ordinary user variable name and $$foo becomes the reserved prefix nobody types by accident — and it makes RULE 31a ($class is compiler-internal, never declare it) enforceable rather than advisory. Two things must be checked before a line moves. Invariant 12 says compiler output is reproducible because scope ids are content-addressed, and CSS dedupe across the two compilers a static build runs depends on it — so whether emitted identifiers feed that hash decides whether every scope id in the repo moves at once. And has to converge in the same pass or the three-tier story is fiction with a nicer name. Checked and clear: there is no $$-in-replacement-string trap, the only .replace() with a $ in its replacement being a '$1' capture reference; and Chrome devtools' $$ console helper is a distinct identifier that a $$foo local cannot shadow, so the single rule that follows is never to emit a bare $$. Blast radius: 421 sites in compiler emit strings and 15 test files that string-match $runtime; zero user .mesa files, since none of these names is author-facing. Attempted 2026-08-24 and reverted — the rename is not a rename, which is the finding. A blanket textual pass over the 430 emit sites went green on the compiler loading and then failed 84–257 tests in three waves, because this compiler encodes its own emitted identifiers in four ways and only one of them is a plain identifier. Regex literals that match its own output: \$parentElement is an ESCAPED dollar, so appending a second one produced \$$parentElement, where the new dollar reads as an end-of-input anchor mid-pattern — and the sibling case \$\$sig is a legitimately doubled name that must NOT move, so the two cannot be told apart by a rule about dollars. String keys paired with property reads: ctx.require('$emit') is a key and ctx.inuse.$emit is a property, so a dot-guard that correctly protects the second silently renames only the first — and the failure is not an error but a binding that stops being emitted at all. A cross-component protocol name: $class is not a scope-local, it is the prop the {class} shorthand travels under, and runtime.js reads it as the string '$class' in restProps' skip set and as $option.$class; renaming it breaks class passthrough between two compiled components. And the runtime's own exports ($onMount, $context, $tick — seven of them) are the public API a composable helper imports and must keep the bare spelling, so they sit in the same file as names that should move. The tree was returned to green (mesa 1264 + 82 + 47, ui 857, sierra 1088, typecheck clean) and nothing of FJS-D132 phases 0-5 was disturbed. What this changes about the fix: it is not a codemod. Each emitted name wants ONE definition the compiler reads — a constant, not a literal repeated across emit strings, regexes and registry keys — and that refactor is the actual work, with the rename falling out of it for free. Doing it the other way round is what was measured here. Also cleared: Invariant 12 does not gate it. cssHash is fed the style content and nothing else, deliberately, so renaming an emitted identifier cannot move a scope id. Probed 2026-08-23, and the answer inverts the assumption: the $-prefixed INTERNALS are clean — $runtime, $dom, $class and $parentElement compile and parse under let, const, var and function alike — while the injected BUILTINS collide, which is FJS-471 and is FJS-D132's to fix. So this item carries no defect behind it and stays S4: it is a naming rule, not a bug. Closed 2026-08-24, on the second attempt and after the ground moved. What made it possible was doing the runtime's exports FIRST: $runtime.$onMount was two namespaces sharing a spelling, and once the export is onMount the local beside it can move without ambiguity. The rename then went through with the four encodings named above handled explicitly — plus a FIFTH the first attempt never reached, which is that $$ inside a .replace() REPLACEMENT STRING collapses to one $, so hoistTemplates emitted $tpl0 = $runtime.template(…) from declarations that read $$tpl0 = $$runtime.template(…); it is a callback now. Two more names turned out to be protocol rather than internal, in the sense FJS-D134 had just ruled: $dom is the key a block factory answers with and runtime.js reads 59 times, and the three COMPILED door members ($context, $inspect, $mounted) are AUTHOR-space names after the pre-parse rewrite, so their injected locals have to keep the bare spelling to be reachable at all. Emitted output now carries no single-$ name; $runtime, $option and $dom are ordinary user variable names, which is the sentence this issue existed to make true. anchor/block/props did NOT converge and that half stays open below. Green: mesa 1265 + 82 + 47, ui 857, sierra 1088, jetty 46, cli 811, typecheck clean
